newsitem.title: USA: Southwest Air's Kelleher cautions would-be mimics.
newsitem.headline: Southwest Air's Kelleher cautions would-be mimics.

text.p: Herb Kelleher, the eccentric Texas businessman whose upstart Southwest Airlines revolutionized the airline industry, has some surprising advice for those hoping to follow his flight path: be conservative.
Very conservative.

While Southwest's high-frequency, low-cost strategy has confounded naysayers throughout its 25-year history and established it as the most consistently profitable U.S. carrier, Kelleher said the success story has been widely misunderstood.
"Very few people realize how conservative we were," Kelleher said in a recent interview, pointing out that Southwest had only 22 planes at the end of its first 10 years.
Kelleher's public image is that of a chain-smoking hellraiser who won the undying loyalty of his employees with humor, eccentric publicity stunts and a relaxed workplace philosophy.
But the 65-year-old chief executive says having fun should not be confused with lax financial stewardship.

"Because we have been so conservative from that standpoint, it always astounds me to see somebody grow from five airplanes to 35 airplanes overnight. That's kind of a daunting thought to me," he said.

Kelleher said the bankruptcy and disappearance of People Express and the severe turbulence at Continental and America West under previous management after a boom period in the 1980s bore witness to the dangers of reckless management.
"If you look at the airlines which went into bankruptcy, went into Chapter 11, there is in most cases a common linkage: they expanded too fast," he said.
But Kelleher conceded there are fewer niche markets available now than when he launched Southwest, setting the standard for budget airlines.
"It's a more difficult thing to do today, I think, because it's no longer a novelty," Kelleher said, adding that Southwest's own expansion also hurts newcomers.
"In more and more instances you are talking about competing directly against Southwest which, as long as we have the best customer service record and the lowest costs, is fairly tough."

Adding to the burdens facing young budget carriers is the recent tightening of regulatory scrutiny, especially after the crash of a ValuJet plane in the Florida Everglades in May that killed all 110 people on board.

Southwest's growth strategy over 25 years has been simple: pick popular, short-haul, city-to-city routes at relatively low-cost airports; offer a high number of regular flights; and drive down prices with a friendly, no-frills service.
The Dallas-based airline often views the car rather than other carriers as its main competitor.

When several major U.S. airlines raised their fares by 10 percent in August to cover the reimposition of a 10 percent excise tax, Southwest kept prices steady on all but its longest routes. One month later, when all its competitors raised fares by an additional 2.5 percent after seeing strong passenger demand, Kelleher again declined.
"We are the low-fare airline. Its that simple," he said.
Southwest now has a fleet of 237 Boeing 737 jets and last year had revenues of $2.87 billion.
This year it launched successful services in and out of Tampa, Ft. Lauderdale and Orlando, and is about to penetrate the Northeast with flights into Providence, RI.
Despite the market and regulatory problems facing young airlines, Kelleher said there are some out there doing a good job, and that Reno Air leads the bunch.
"Reno has been restrained in the way it has expanded," he said. "They have been more conservative not only in expansion, but also in the number of competitors that they take on simultaneously."
Picking your battles, Kelleher said, is key to survival for new entrants, and having low costs can be of little use unless you have the liquidity needed for long-term battles over lucrative markets.
"You have to be able to slug it for a long period of time, be in condition for a 15-round championship match, not a six-round Golden Gloves fight," he said.
